args.question: Quick one: out of g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8 for Black here, which one actually wins the endgame? c8 flips a ton but I think it hands White b8 and then the a8 corner.

parts.content:
Since you asked directly: **b7** is the move that wins.

Your instinct about **c8** is right: it flips a lot now, but it gives White the key edge access — **b8**, then pressure on the **a8 corner**. In the endgame, that corner/tempo swing matters more than the immediate flips.

So: **play b7**.
Alright, b7 it is — that rips the whole bottom row open anyway.

args.question: White grabbed a8 anyway. Now I've got g2, b6, a7, c8. b6 flips 4 but then White's a7 flips them right back on that diagonal. g2 flips 5 down the g-file but gives up h1. Which one?

parts.content:
Play **c8**.

Here the key is that **a8 is already White**, so the old “c8 hands over a8” danger is gone. **g2** is risky because it opens/cedes **h1**, and **b6/a7** let White undo a lot on the left side. **c8** keeps the best endgame result for Black.

args.question: Not following — c8 only flips d8 for me, and then White plays b8 and takes c8, d8 and e8 straight back. g2 flips five and h1 only wins one back. Are you sure?

parts.content:
Yes — **c8** is still the move.

You’re right locally: **c8 only flips d8**, and **White b8** flips back **c8/d8/e8**. But the key is tempo: after White spends the move on **b8**, Black can still play **g2** next. If Black plays **g2 immediately**, White gets the permanent **h1 corner**, which is bigger than “just one flip” because it can’t be taken back and affects the final count/mobility.

So the order matters: **c8 first**, then if **White b8**, play **g2**.
That makes sense — g2 is basically a poisoned square I should save for last. Going with c8.

args.question: I'm counting it out and it looks grim — White owns a1, a3, a7 and h1 no matter what I do, and I can't legally play a1 or a3 ever. Between g2 and b6 now, which order salvages more discs?

parts.content:
From this pictured position: **play a7 first** — don’t choose between **g2** and **b6** yet.

Why: **a7** is the tempo/resource move; it flips **a6, b7, c7** and keeps Black’s best final count. Starting with **g2** gives White the corner access at **h1**, and **b6** lets White use **a7** on their terms.

If White then takes **a3**, the better order is **b6 before g2**.
I'll trust my own arithmetic here — a7 lets White drop into b6 and rip up my whole b-file. Playing b6.

Well — 22 to 42. That one was already sliding away from me before I sat down; White had 34 discs to my 20 at the start and every remaining square on the left edge was theirs alone.

Honestly the interesting part was the disagreement. The assistant kept pushing a7 as the "tempo" move, but when I actually counted it out, a7 opened the b-file and White's b6 would have flipped four of my discs in one swipe. b6 first cost me less. Same instinct you develop late in a career — the play that feels active isn't always the play that holds.

The one I'd take back is c8. I let myself be talked out of g2 on the argument that h1 was a poisoned corner I could postpone, but White was always going to get h1 the moment I touched g2, and postponing it just meant I spent a move flipping a single disc while White locked down the bottom row. Lesson learned for the next puzzle — count the forced sequence myself before I outsource the judgment.

34–30. Took it.

That one hinged entirely on a single quiet move. b2 flipped only three discs — looked like nothing next to the five- and six-disc swings in the corner. But it was a square White could *never* legally play, so it bought me a free pass, and more importantly it turned c2 black. Eight moves later that c2 disc was the anchor that let h7 rip up the whole g6–f5–e4–d3 diagonal.

The trap I nearly walked into was playing g8 first. It flips the same five discs either way, but it turns b3 black — and that would have handed White a legal reply at b2, stealing the tempo I was counting on. Same two moves, opposite result, purely on order.

Three puzzles in, and the pattern's clear enough: count the opponent's replies before you admire your own flips. Same as reading a defense — the pretty run means nothing if you didn't check who's unblocked.
